stories.summary: In 1958, farmers complained to the Chinese state that sparrows were a nuisance. Chairman Mao ordered them killed, and sparrows were hunted down all over China. But sparrows ate locusts. Once the sparrows were gone, the locusts multiplied and destroyed China's crops. The famine that followed killed about forty-five million people, in what became known as the Great Leap Forward.
stories.insight: This is Amit's standard example of Adam Smith's 'man of system', who moves one piece on society's chessboard and forgets that every piece moves on its own. Complex systems punish top-down tinkering, and the costs can run into millions of lives. It is the conservative warning to respect complexity, shown at its most extreme.
stories.quote: Sparrows played a role in the ecosystem. They ate locusts, right? When the sparrows died out, the locusts proliferated and they destroyed all the crops of China.

stories.topic: Ambedkar Keeps 'Socialist' Out of the Preamble
stories.summary: In 1948, K.T. Shah moved to add three words to the Preamble. Ambedkar rejected two of them, 'secular' and 'socialist'. On secularism, he said it was already written into the Constitution's articles, so stating it was unnecessary. On socialism, he said a constitution is only a mechanism for regulating the organs of the state. How society is organised must be left to the people to decide according to time and circumstances. Indira Gandhi added both words in the mid-1970s. Today every political party registering in India must pledge allegiance to socialism. That means Amit and Ajay could not start a party without betraying their beliefs. S.V. Raju of the Swatantra Party fought this rule in court for years and lost.
stories.insight: A founder of the Constitution warned that writing an ideology into it would take away the people's freedom to choose a better arrangement later. The later amendment that overrode him still decides who is allowed to enter Indian politics.
stories.quote: we would be unable to start a party because we'd have to pledge to socialism, which fundamentally goes against everything we believe in.

stories.topic: The Wrong Preamble at the CAA Protests
stories.summary: Amit opposed the CAA and was delighted to see young people across India marching with the Preamble. But many of them carried the amended version with the word 'socialist' in it, not Ambedkar's original. He wanted to ask whether they knew what the word means. In his view, socialism kept India poor for decades longer than necessary.
stories.insight: People can hold up a document as a symbol without knowing its history. The protesters treated 'socialist' as a common noun meaning 'good for society', when it is a proper noun for a specific program that Ambedkar himself kept out.
stories.quote: many of them were holding the wrong preamble. They were not holding Ambedkar's preamble, they were holding Indira's preamble, which has the word socialist in it.

stories.summary: In 1790 Edmund Burke wrote Reflections on the Revolution in France. He did not object to the revolution's ideals. He warned that its means were disastrous. For the 'History of Ideas' webinar in their Life Lessons course, Amit invented postcards between the two men, built from real quotes. Robespierre tells Burke, roughly, to shut up, calls him an old fogey and asks what he is even trying to conserve. Burke replies, 'Bro, I warned you, I hope you're around to read this.' By then Robespierre had himself been purged, after doing a fair amount of purging.
stories.insight: Ends and means are separate questions. Good intentions pursued by tearing everything down tend to destroy the people who pursue them. Burke's case was that institutions and norms have survived a kind of natural selection, so they exist for a reason.
stories.quote: Here's Burke's reply to Robespierre, where he says that bro, I warned you, I hope you're around to read this.

stories.summary: Amit's real heroes of the freedom struggle come before Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and Ambedkar. They are the moderates of the late 19th and early 20th century: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar and Ranade. The usual story sets them against extremists like Tilak. But the Scottish statesman James Keir Hardie observed that the two camps were not far apart. Then Gandhi arrived, a 'black swan' who broke with everything before him.
stories.insight: Amit says the moderates were liberal in their ends and conservative in their means. They wanted a freer and more empowered India, but they worked step by step instead of through random violence. He uses this as a template for reform anywhere.
stories.quote: the moderates were extreme in their moderation, and the extremists were moderate in their extremism.

stories.summary: 'Tiki-taka' is now the name for Pep Guardiola's possession football, which descends from Johan Cruyff's Total Football. But Guardiola did not coin the term and hates it. The broadcaster Andrés Montes coined it during the 2006 World Cup, before Guardiola was a coach, to mock Spain's pointless passing. Athletic Bilbao's coach Javier Clemente used it the same dismissive way. The insult later got attached to Barcelona's style.
stories.insight: Amit offers this as a parallel to 'liberal' and 'conservative', both of which began as cuss words thrown at people who never chose them. A label's origin can be the opposite of how it ends up being worn.
stories.quote: But the truth is Guardiola hates the term. He didn't coin it.

stories.summary: In 1907 or 1947, land carried deep emotional weight in India, especially in old North Indian machismo, because owning land meant wealth and income. A man with fifty thousand acres outranked a man with ten thousand. Today India's wealth comes from building businesses like Infosys and Reliance. Land is nice to have but neither necessary nor sufficient for success. The old landed classes did not want this change.
stories.insight: This shows why 'liberal' and 'conservative' became opposites. From Adam Smith to Marx, thinkers saw capitalism and globalisation as a 'wild west wind' that would tear up the feudal order. The people who benefited from aristocracy, land, religion and family hierarchy fought to keep it, and that defence became one meaning of conservatism.
stories.quote: A person with fifty thousand acres was a bigger person than a person with 10,000 acres. Okay, and so on. But look at the modern world. The wealth of today's India is not created out of land.

stories.summary: John Locke argued that we are born owning ourselves, and that the rights to life, free speech and property follow from that. At the end of the 18th century Mary Wollstonecraft read Locke and drew the next conclusion: if everyone has these inalienable rights, women have them too. In a world where 'he' and 'him' were the default for all people, this was a radical idea, and modern feminism grew out of it.
stories.insight: Modern feminism grew directly out of classical liberalism's idea of individual rights. A principle stated in general terms tends to be extended to people its author never had in mind.
stories.quote: if all of us have these inalienable rights, then it's not just the men. It's also the women, which was a radical thought in those times

stories.summary: At eighteen, Amit carried Das Kapital around in his college bag for a few days, feeling cool and intellectual. He had actually read Marx and Engels when young. He jokes that, thankfully, it did not completely destroy his brain.
stories.insight: Total theories are seductive to the young because they seem to explain everything, and they come with a flattering self-image. Amit's later views came from being 'mugged by reality': watching outcomes rather than intentions.
stories.quote: for a few days in my bag I carried around with me Das Kapital by Marx and Engels. Yeah. Because I've actually read these books when I was young. But thank God they didn't completely destroy my brain.

stories.summary: At the end of an otherwise excellent episode of The Seen and the Unseen, a guest used 'neoliberal' as a slur. Amit asked her to define it, and she could not. He won't link the episode, but he now stops taking people seriously when they use the word.
stories.insight: If someone cannot define a label they use as an insult, the label is doing their thinking for them. A useful habit in any debate is to ask the other person to define their terms.
stories.quote: she used the term neoliberal at the end of a really great episode and I kinda challenged her on it and she couldn't even define it.

stories.topic: The Friend Who Dropped 'Proud Right Winger'
stories.summary: A dear friend of both hosts used to describe himself on Twitter as 'a proud right winger', meaning he supported free markets. About eleven or twelve years ago he removed it, because the word's connotations had changed and now covered much more than economics.
stories.insight: You can stay exactly where you are while the label you wear moves. Tribes you do not control can change what your self-description means.
stories.quote: a friend of ours, a very dear friend of both of us, who on his Twitter bio used to say, a proud right winger. And he immediately took that off, I think about eleven, twelve years ago, because the connotation of the word completely changed.

stories.topic: The Professor Who Ranted Only Off the Record
stories.summary: Amit once had an openly left-wing American academic on his show. When the subject of wokeism came up, the guest asked him not to raise it on air. He said he would rant and rave about it privately, but as a professor at a US university there were things he could not say on the record.
stories.insight: Amit cites this as a sign that even the left has started to recoil from wokeism, while privately disagreeing still feels unsafe in public. It is a small view of how an ideological climate can silence its own sympathisers.
stories.quote: I will rant and rave off the record, but I'm a professor in a university in the USA. There are things I cannot say on the record.

recommendations.creator: Arnold Kling
recommendations.context: First book on the closing reading list.
recommendations.reason: Explains why political discourse is broken: progressives argue from equality, libertarians from freedom and conservatives from tradition, so they talk past each other. The book teaches you to grant the other side's first principles and argue on their terms, which is how minds actually change.

recommendations.creator: Richard Pipes
recommendations.context: Reading list, after the chapters on Marxism, socialism and communism.
recommendations.reason: A slim volume on what actually happened under communism, linking ideas to actions to consequences. Amit suggests it as a way into Pipes's other books and into historians like Robert Conquest.

recommendations.item: The Libertarian Mind: A Manifesto for Freedom
recommendations.creator: David Boaz
recommendations.context: Promised during the libertarianism chapter and named on the reading list. Boaz is the source of the 'daddy, mommy, adult' line.
recommendations.reason: Boaz is one of Amit's modern heroes, a great thinker who died recently. The book is a clear statement of the case for freedom.

recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Reading list. Amit reveres Sowell so much that he is afraid to invite him on his show.
recommendations.reason: Explains how ideologies take shape and come into being. Amit's broader advice is to read all of Sowell's books.

recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Reading list.
recommendations.reason: Amit says that by the end of the book he had become a much clearer thinker about economics.

recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Reading list, under 'everything by Milton Friedman'.
recommendations.reason: Part of the foundational reading that shaped Amit's understanding of free markets and freedom.

recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman and Rose Friedman
recommendations.context: Reading list. Co-written by Milton Friedman with his wife Rose.
recommendations.reason: A core Friedman text in the 'recommend everything by him' list.

recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Reading list, alongside the book. Two seasons, easy to watch on YouTube.
recommendations.reason: An accessible, watchable version of Friedman's case for freedom.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Reading list. Discussed earlier in their 'four papers that changed the world' episode and echoed in the statism chapter.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterpiece full of lightbulb moments. It explains why no planner can replace the spontaneous order of prices.

recommendations.item: The Collected Works of Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Reading list.
recommendations.reason: 'The man who really turned me on to freedom.' The title of Amit's podcast The Seen and the Unseen comes from one of Bastiat's essays.

recommendations.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the socialism chapter. More than sixty volumes, free online, to be linked from the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Free and 'amazing to read'. Reading them shows the arc of Ambedkar's thinking, including how he became much more pro-capitalism by the early 1950s.

recommendations.creator: Mahatma Gandhi
recommendations.context: Named with Ambedkar's collected works as a free online resource.
recommendations.reason: Ninety-nine volumes, free to read. Amit calls it a priceless resource.

recommendations.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
recommendations.context: Cited in the socialism chapter, where Ambedkar asks the socialists whether economic reform is possible without first reforming the social order.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it Ambedkar's 'great masterpiece of a book'. It is an early challenge to class-only thinking that puts caste at the centre.

recommendations.item: Reflections on the Revolution in France
recommendations.creator: Edmund Burke
recommendations.context: The 1790 pamphlet Amit uses to define conservatism in its serious sense.
recommendations.reason: The founding text for the idea that means matter. Burke accepts the revolutionaries' ideals but warns that you cannot burn institutions to the ground and expect good outcomes.

recommendations.item: The Open Society and Its Enemies
recommendations.creator: Karl Popper
recommendations.context: Quoted in the nationalism chapter as 'his great book'.
recommendations.reason: Source of Popper's diagnosis that nationalism appeals to tribal instinct and lets people escape the strain of individual responsibility.

recommendations.creator: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
recommendations.context: Raised while Ajay explains why liberal and conservative became opposites.
recommendations.reason: Ajay rejects its prescriptions but says entire chunks are 'absolutely brilliant' on how capitalism and globalisation would tear up the feudal order.

recommendations.creator: Yael Tamir
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the nationalism chapter. Amit reviewed it and will link the review.
recommendations.reason: A serious scholarly case for nationalism. Amit disagrees, and reading it alongside his review gives both sides. The review ends by arguing that those who divide us are the true anti-nationals.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Arnold Kling
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Kling discussed The Three Languages of Politics on Amit's show.
recommendations.reason: An audio companion to the book. Here Kling adds a fourth tribe, Trumpism/MAGA, to his original three.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Jerry Rao on Indian conservatism
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Raised in the conservatism chapter. Jerry Rao has written a book on Indian conservatism.
recommendations.reason: A lively disagreement in which Amit argues that Burkean conservatism barely exists in India. He recommends it to anyone who thinks he never argues with his guests.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Nitin Pai on liberal nationalism
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the nationalism chapter.
recommendations.reason: Pai, whom both hosts admire, defends 'liberal nationalism' and Amit argues against it at length. Amit admits he might be wrong and leaves listeners to judge.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: From an audio podcast Amit used to do, to be linked in the show notes, mentioned in the liberalism chapter.
recommendations.reason: Wollstonecraft is one of Amit's great heroes. The episode covers how she extended Locke's rights to women and so began modern feminism.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode on Populism
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referred to instead of defining populism again in this episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit loves the episode. Populism is not 'what is popular' but a dangerous package of beliefs and methods that is rising worldwide alongside nationalism.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything Episodes 25 and 26 on the role of the state
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited in the liberalism and libertarianism chapters and on the closing list.
recommendations.reason: They set out the liberal worldview and how to think about what the state may do, given the violence it uses.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything Episode 10 on Freedom
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited in the socialism chapter and on the closing list.
recommendations.reason: Covers Nehru's Fabian socialism and why freedom is the right lens for thinking about Indian policy.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode on four papers that changed the world
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced in the statism chapter and the reading list.
recommendations.reason: Explains Hayek's insight that prices create a spontaneous order no central planner can replicate.

core_ideas.explanation: A political label has a dictionary meaning and a separate meaning as a tribal brand. Quoting the dictionary to defend 'liberal' or 'socialist' misses that the label has picked up its own, often contradictory, baggage. Labels also change over time and between places, so a clear conversation needs both sides to say which meaning they intend.
core_ideas.quote: I know many liberals who are not liberal. I know many progressive people who espouse policies that would actually set us back and not take us forward. I know many conservatives who hold radical views, right? I know many nationalists who in my view are anti-national

core_ideas.explanation: Any label that confers prestige attracts people who want the prestige without the beliefs. Once those people outnumber the believers, the label comes to mean its opposite. Amit says grifters took 'liberal' and are now taking 'libertarian'. This is part of why he now refuses all labels.
core_ideas.quote: All labels that bestow any kind of prestige or virtue upon the bearer eventually come to mean the opposite, as grifters and opportunists outnumber the believers.

core_ideas.concept: Cause, Movement, Racket — and Ideas Aren't Guilty by Association
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay notes that every great idea starts as a cause, becomes a movement and ends up a racket as political formations grow around it. He separates the idea from its followers: if Trump believes X, that says nothing about whether X is true. Ideas should be judged on their merits, not by who holds them.
core_ideas.quote: An idea is not responsible for the person that believes in it. Ideas should be argued and judged and debated around a variety of intellectual aspects, but this is not a gotcha

core_ideas.concept: Tribalism vs the Minor Matter of Being Correct
core_ideas.explanation: People who join an ideological tribe take on all its dogmas and follow it wherever it drifts. Amit's example is how so many conservatives and libertarians lined up behind Trump once he took over the Republican Party. He sees the same pattern in India. Ajay's remedy is to care about being right: forecasting what an intervention will actually do and judging it after ten, fifty or a hundred years.
core_ideas.quote: being correct matters. It's not just all ideology, but there's something very sad about the world that the tribal instinct is so powerful.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit lays out their shared priors before defining anything. (1) The world is positive-sum, so poverty and inequality call for different, even opposite, policies. (2) Top-down design that worked in small hunter-gatherer tribes fails at the scale of a society. (3) Judge actions by outcomes, not intentions, since every ideology has fine intentions. (4) Freedom is good in itself and also produces the best outcomes, so think in terms of individuals, not groups. Ajay's illustration of point three is Hitler: no one did more damage to the 'Germanic peoples' than the man who championed them most fiercely.
core_ideas.quote: if your objective was the glory and furtherance of the Germanic peoples, of German DNA, then there was no bigger disaster for that than the man who espoused this the most.

core_ideas.concept: Self-Ownership, Negative Rights and Positive Rights
core_ideas.explanation: Locke's foundational right is self-ownership. The rights to life, free speech and property follow from it. Isaiah Berlin later called these 'negative' rights because they only require others not to do something to you. 'Positive rights' such as a right to food or free broadband require someone else to provide them, which means taxing others and so infringing their negative rights. Amit's point is not that the state should never feed people, for example in a famine. It is that calling entitlements 'rights' muddles every debate.
core_ideas.quote: So a right to food is a positive right. If I say I have a right to food, that means the state has to feed me

core_ideas.explanation: Rights mean nothing unless someone enforces them, so we need a state. Thomas Paine called government a 'necessary evil'. It is evil because it holds a monopoly on violence and lives on coerced taxes, so to protect our rights we must give some of them up. Amit concludes that every ideology is really an argument about how much state violence is justified. Adam Smith's version of the minimal state is 'peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice'.
core_ideas.quote: I call it the great liberal paradox, that for our rights to have meaning we must give up some of them, right? And this is fundamental to understanding political theory.

core_ideas.concept: How 'Liberal' Flipped in America — and Why 'Libertarian' Was Born
core_ideas.explanation: Smith probably first used 'liberal' politically, writing of a 'liberal system of free exportation and free importation'. In the 20th century, American liberals took up positive rights and an expanding welfare state to fix inequality, while Europe kept the older meaning. Asked by Ajay, Amit agrees that small-state thinkers then adopted 'libertarian' for themselves. In effect, 'classical liberal' and 'libertarian' describe the same old-school liberalism.
core_ideas.quote: it was no longer a limited government, the night watchman state, which was a necessary evil. But instead it was an all encompassing Maibaap which had to feed you and clothe you.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay separates two impulses in the word. One defends an established order, whether religion, family, social hierarchy or oligarchy, often because its defenders benefit from it. The other is a more sophisticated stance: the world is too complex for grand coercive schemes, and means matter. Amit rejects the first, because the world needs radical change, and fully accepts the second.
core_ideas.quote: It's a respect for the richness and complexity of the world. It's a mistrust of any grand scheme.

core_ideas.explanation: Burke's central lesson separates ends from means. Change the world, by all means, but remember that institutions and norms have survived for reasons and cannot be burnt down without consequences. Amit argues that India has little of this Burkean conservatism. What gets called conservatism here is either preserving the past for its own sake or a radical, divisive tribalism that goes against India's assimilative traditions.
core_ideas.quote: please understand that the edifices that exist, the institutions that exist, the norms that exist exist for a particular reason. They have gone through natural selection, they've passed the test of time.

core_ideas.concept: Marxism as Theory, Socialism as Path, Communism as Destination
core_ideas.explanation: Marxism, from the Communist Manifesto (1848) and Das Kapital (1867), divides the world into a bourgeoisie that oppresses and exploits a proletariat. The predicted revolution passes through a 'dictatorship of the proletariat'. Amit lists the criticisms: it reduces everything to class (Weber, Popper); its predicted collapse of capitalism never came (Popper, Fukuyama); it ignores race, gender and caste (Foucault, intersectional thinkers); it goes against human nature (Isaiah Berlin, and E.O. Wilson's 'Great idea, wrong species'); and it can only be reached through mass violence (Arendt, Aron). Communism's destination is no private property and 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'. Amit says this amounts to equality of poverty, and that it was markets, not communism, that made China rich.
core_ideas.quote: You can think of Marxism as a theory, socialism as a path, communism as a destination.

core_ideas.explanation: A successful ideology offers a frame into which every event can be fitted, so it seems to explain everything. That is what makes it so attractive to the young, and it is also a warning sign. A theory that can absorb any evidence is not really being tested by any.
core_ideas.quote: any ideological theory that works will appear to explain everything and therefore is deeply seductive to the young.

core_ideas.explanation: Marx predicted that capitalism's booms and busts would grow worse, and the Great Depression seemed to confirm it. Amit adds that it is now understood to have been caused by state action, as Thomas Sowell has written. Ajay notes that no shock since has been as large, and that 2008 was relatively small. Booms and busts are a normal part of how capitalism works. As Robert Lucas observed, they are trivial next to the steady compounding of growth. Natural experiments like North versus South Korea and East versus West Germany settle the question.
core_ideas.quote: when you correctly draw the graph, the fluctuations appear irrelevant. The dominant phenomenon is the growth.

core_ideas.explanation: Liberalism takes the individual as its unit. Marxism, and any ideology built on group averages, essentialises people who contain multitudes. Amit cites Ayn Rand: the smallest minority is the individual. Ajay adds that people are heterogeneous, and averages like 'men are taller than women' flatten that richness.
core_ideas.quote: I would even say don't use the word society when you talk about the good of society. It's really dangerous. What we should put at the center is individual rights and the rights of every individual.

core_ideas.concept: Socialism Is a Program, Not a Synonym for 'Good for Society'
core_ideas.explanation: In political theory, socialism has four features: public ownership of resources, redistribution towards equal outcomes, a centrally planned economy, and attractive stated intentions that it fails to deliver. Indians tend to read it as the Hindi 'samajwad', meaning broadly 'on the side of society', which Amit happily accepts. As a proper noun, though, it describes the Fabian-style planning that kept India poor. Ajay adds that socialism can only be built by crushing individual rights, so it cannot coexist with constitutional liberal democracy.
core_ideas.quote: Socialist doesn't mean what is good for society. You know, please understand the implications. Socialism kept us poor for decades longer than necessary.

core_ideas.concept: From Revolutionary Violence to One-Party Rule
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay asks why state ownership of everything always ends in one-party dictatorship. Amit, thinking aloud, says a movement that accepts coercion as a way to take power will use it to keep power. Once you have built a state strong enough to jail every opponent, you have no reason to give it up.
core_ideas.quote: once you decide that violence and coercion are an acceptable way to come to power, then they axiomatically become an acceptable way to stay in power.

core_ideas.explanation: Statism is not a separate ideology. It is an attitude many ideologies share: the belief that society can be run from the top down. Adam Smith's 'man of system' falls in love with his ideal plan and arranges people like pieces on a chessboard. Real people have their own motives, and when those clash with the plan, society falls into disorder.
core_ideas.quote: in the great chessboard of human society every single piece has a principle of motion of its own, altogether different from that which the legislature might choose to impress upon it.

core_ideas.explanation: Libertarians come in two kinds. Anarchists think norms are enough and no state is needed. Minarchists, which includes Amit, accept a limited night-watchman state. Amit quotes David Boaz: conservatives want to be your daddy, liberals want to be your mommy, and libertarians want to treat you as an adult. Amit's test is that two consenting adults who harm no one should be left alone, both in the bedroom and in the marketplace.
core_ideas.quote: the conservative right will object at what you do in the bedroom and the left will object to what you do in the marketplace. And I think that that is deeply, deeply incoherent.

core_ideas.concept: Left and Right: Seating Chart Turned Shorthand
core_ideas.explanation: The terms come from the French National Assembly. Those seated on the left opposed the monarchy and the feudal order, and those on the right defended them. Amit describes today's left as using the state as the instrument of change, with coercion and zero-sum thinking built in, though it is often right about social freedoms. Today's right combines both kinds of conservatism with support for free markets. Ajay once mapped left and right onto inequality versus growth. He now notes Lant Pritchett's 'anti-growth coalition' in every country, and that anti-growth policies increasingly come from the right. In India, Amit says, the label makes no sense, because every party is against freedom in both domains.
core_ideas.quote: All our parties are left of centre when it comes to economics and right of center in a bad way when it comes to society.

core_ideas.explanation: Patriotism is loving your country. Nationalism defines the nation by 'othering' some people and plays on hardwired tribal instincts. Tagore called nationalism a great menace. Popper said it appeals to passion and prejudice and lets people escape the strain of individual responsibility. Ramachandra Guha, quoted by Amit, says a patriot works to make his country less violent, less poor and less exploitative, while a nationalist wants to bomb everybody else. Amit proposes Varma's Sixth Law: anyone who calls others anti-national is the true anti-national.
core_ideas.quote: While a patriot strives to make his or her country a better place, a less violent place, a less poverty ridden place, and a less exploitative place. A nationalist wants to bomb everybody else. He doesn't care how bad his own country is.

core_ideas.explanation: In 'What is Hindutva' (1925), Savarkar defined a Hindu as someone whose homeland and land of worship are both India. Amit calls the definition masterful but toxic, because it neatly includes Jains and Buddhists while excluding Muslims and Christians, and no one questions the premise. Aakar Patel's test, which Amit puts to listeners, is that for most ideologies you can say what they are for, but for Hindutva you can only say what it is against.
core_ideas.quote: Shruti Kapila described Hindutva as a theory of violence in search of a history. And Savarkar made an attempt to give it a history and a theory.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay observes that intensely nationalistic people are often privately anxious about India's weaknesses and about the success of advanced economies. Confident people relax and engage with others as equals. He contrasts this with how Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru combined being Indian with openness to the world. Gandhi, for instance, was deeply influenced by Tolstoy and read the New Testament closely.
core_ideas.quote: If you're actually strong, if you're actually capable, then you will relax, then you will engage with others as equals, there'll be a happy and healthy give and take.

core_ideas.explanation: 'Woke' originally meant being awake to social injustice, a meaning Amit embraces. As an ideology, he argues, it succeeds Marxism. It keeps the oppressor/oppressed frame and multiplies the categories through intersectionality. People are fixed by their identity at birth as victim or oppressor, which leads to an 'Olympics of victimhood'. Liberalism respects the individual's complexity, while wokeism essentialises it. Amit thinks peak woke is behind us.
core_ideas.quote: wokeism begins where liberalism ends.

core_ideas.concept: Argue From the Other Side's First Principles
core_ideas.explanation: Following Arnold Kling, Amit argues that progressives (equality), libertarians (freedom) and conservatives (tradition) talk past each other by repeating their own values. If you care about freedom and the other person cares about equality, start by agreeing on the goal, such as reducing poverty, and then argue from history and evidence about what will achieve it. That is how Bayesian updating actually happens.
core_ideas.quote: our discourse has been destroyed today because of a fundamental problem. That we are not talking to each other, we are talking past each other.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After Ajay promises listeners a 'beautiful storyline', Amit replies: 'there is one way in which you are like a socialist. Which is that you promise a lot. And I'm worried if [I] can deliver.'
Introducing Varma's Fifth Law, Amit asks Ajay: 'Do you know the first four laws? No, not even one. Neither do I.' He promises to 'figure out three more in between later'.

Amit imagines the biologist E.O. Wilson telling Karl Marx, who died long before Wilson was born: 'dude, great freaking theory, man, but sell it to the ants.' Then he adds that ants are already like that, so you don't need to sell them anything.
Ajay's Soviet joke: they justified the destruction by saying you have to break eggs to make an omelette, and then someone asks, 'We broke a lot of eggs. Where's the omelette?'

Ajay: 'He who has not been a Marxist as a child has no heart. And he who is a Marxist as an adult has no brain.' Amit scolds him for using 'left' before they have defined it, telling him not to use words they haven't explained yet, 'which basically would mean don't say anything'.

Ajay on human inequality: 'Everybody is not born with an Elo of 2830... My Elo sucks and you just got to accept this. We're all different. I'm not Magnus.' Later Amit says that when they play chess the plan may work 'even if you're not 2830'.

Amit on communism: he'd presumably be allowed to keep his iPad, though the state could take it any time, 'Except that there would be no iPad because I would not be rich enough in a communist society to buy an iPad unless I was kind of running the show.'
On being unable to register a party without pledging to socialism: 'which of course we never will, because we are thinkers and not doers. No, we are doers but in a different way.'
Amit on why he dropped the libertarian label: 'I don't like labels, and I also don't like other libertarians because they're not libertarian.'

On Bill Clinton's sensible pro-market presidency: 'One could say his personal failing was he was too liberal with his affections, but leaving that aside.' This calls back to the episode's opening point about 'liberal with her affections' as a common-noun usage.
Amit on doing a full episode about wokeism someday: 'after which I will get lynched and the show will end. So maybe that's well into the future.'
After the tiki-taka story: 'Friedrich Hayek, Milton Friedman, Pep Guardiola, these are all geniuses, and we should respect and venerate them.'

Show notes: 'The full show notes will follow soon. Right now, we are under the sway of an ideology called Procrastinatism, which is turning us into Incompletists. Do you think we should start a party? Bring your own balloons.'

Etymology: 'liberal' comes from the Latin liber/liberalis, meaning generous and befitting a free person. That is the source of everyday phrases like 'liberal with her affections' or 'liberal with his wealth'.
Hobbes's 'nasty, brutish and short' and Thomas Paine's description of government as 'a necessary evil' in Common Sense. Amit says Paine's is where the phrase first comes from.

Adam Smith probably first used 'liberal' in a political sense in The Wealth of Nations, writing of 'the liberal system of free exportation and free importation'. Amit adds: 'So globalization Zindabad.'

Ajay criticises Subhas Chandra Bose, whom he describes as an ICS topper who 'wanted to pick up guns and change the order'. He argues that anti-colonial movements fought with guns left a legacy of violence that ripped up their societies.
Nehru was 'under the sway' of the Fabian Society, which he encountered in England, and so became a Fabian socialist, which led to India's five-year plans.

Chandra Bhan Prasad, a Dalit scholar who has appeared on The Seen and the Unseen, says his heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith. Amit cites this when explaining how Ambedkar's later thinking moved towards capitalism.
Ajay cites the night-time satellite image of North versus South Korea, along with East versus West Germany, as natural experiments in which the socialist 'treatment' failed.

Theodore Roosevelt left the Republican Party in 1912 to found a short-lived Progressive Party. Amit lists him with Du Bois and Woodrow Wilson as early self-described progressives, before FDR took up the label after the Great Depression.
